unit.unitOverview: Talk about what is not true, and what you wish were. Work out a cause from the evidence and say how sure you are. Say what ought to have been done, and choose whether that is a finding about a system or an accusation about a person. Then say what a precaution was meant to prevent.
unit.learningPath:
The lesson: listen first, then read it back.
Words: five groups, 29 words. Listen and say each one.
Patterns: 5 cards. Read the one done for you before you try.
Reading: an account of a review, a language guide and a set of findings.
Questions: 10 about the three texts.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, listen back.
Writing: four tasks, each with a model.
Practice and the check: 7 exercises, then 12 questions.
functions: Talk about a situation that is not true, and what you would do
Complain about something without accusing anybody
Say how certain you are about a cause, and why
Say what ought to have been done, without blaming unfairly
Explain what a precaution was meant to prevent
Tell a finding from a guess in somebody else's report
Say how likely something is: plausible, feasible, remote

visual.lectureScript:
This is the least familiar unit in the level. Four of its five patterns are new outright.
It is about the space between what you know and what you are guessing, and about how English marks the difference.

Start with a form Unit 5 deliberately left alone.
Unit 5 taught the real conditionals. If it rains tomorrow, I will take the bus. That might happen.
This is the unreal one. If I had the time, I would rewrite it.
I do not have the time. That is the whole point of the sentence.
Look at what is doing the work. The if half is in the PAST, and nothing about the sentence is past.
That past tense is not about time. It is a way of marking something as not true, and once you see that, the next card follows from it.
The usual warning carries over from Unit 5. No would in the if half. If I would have the time is not English, exactly as if it will rain was not.
And one small thing worth the effort. In careful English it is if I were you, not if I was you. That were survives only here, which is why it sounds strange anywhere else.

The second card uses the same trick.
I wish I knew what happened. Past tense, about now, marking it as not so.
That is how English complains about a situation without complaining about a person, which makes it very useful at work.
There are three shapes. For a fact, the past simple: I wish I knew. For an ability, could: I wish I could help.
And for somebody else's behaviour, would: I wish they would reply.
That last one is a complaint, and it is the only one that takes would.
You cannot say I wish I would know, because your own behaviour is yours to change.

The third card is a job for modals that no unit below this one touches.
You know must for obligation and can't for inability. They have a completely separate use, and it is about how sure you are.
It must be the seal. Nothing else touches that line.
It can't be the supplier. They made no delivery that week.
It might be either, if you do not yet know.
There is one trap here and it is worth hearing twice.
The opposite of must be is CAN'T be. It is not mustn't be.
Mustn't be means it is forbidden, which belongs to the other job entirely.
And to make any of these about the past, add have and the participle. It must have been the seal.
What these do, which a flat statement does not, is tell the reader you are reasoning rather than reporting.
The seal failed is a finding. It must have been the seal is a deduction. A good report keeps those apart.

The fourth card is the one that matters most outside a classroom.
Should have, plus a past participle. It did not happen, and it ought to have.
I should have checked the log. He shouldn't have moved the trolley.
Here is the thing to understand about it. The same grammar does two very different jobs. It apologises, and it accuses.
And there is one choice that decides which.
I should have checked the log names me. The log should have been checked names nobody.
The reading in this unit is about somebody who sat through a review where four people took turns saying what should have been noticed.
Every one of them was right, and none of it had been obvious at the time.
The chair said something worth keeping. It should have been noticed is a finding about a system. You should have noticed it is an accusation about a person. And people say the second when they mean the first.
So make that choice on purpose. Use the passive when you mean the procedure, and name somebody only when you mean them.
Hindsight makes everything look obvious. There is a word for that, and it is hindsight.

The last card finishes the purpose set.
Unit 7 gave you so that. Here is the rest: in order to, so as to, and the plain to that you use every day.
What none of them covered is the negative. What did you do it to AVOID?
We left early so as not to miss the train. Or in order not to.
Not to not miss it, and not for not missing it. Both of those are common and neither is English.
And one more, which learners use for purpose by mistake.
In case. We took a spare in case the first one failed.
That is not an aim. Failing was not what you wanted. It is a possibility you prepared for.
So that is the aim. In case is the possibility.
Start with the words. Say each one aloud before you move on.

readings.title: Everything Looks Obvious Afterwards
readings.passageScript:
I sat through a review last month that taught me something about hindsight.
Four people took turns saying what should have been noticed, and every one of them was right.
The log should have been checked. The brake should have been tested. Somebody should have asked why the trolley was there.
All true, and all of it obvious, and none of it obvious at the time.
Here is what I keep thinking about.
If you had asked me the week before, I would not have picked any of those three out of the forty other things nobody checked that week.
That is not a defence. It is a description of how hindsight works.
Once you know which thing failed, that thing becomes the one that was obviously going to.
The person chairing it said something useful near the end.
He said that it should have been noticed is a finding about a system.
You should have noticed it is an accusation about a person.
And people say the second when they mean the first.
So now I write it in the passive when I mean the system, and I name somebody only when I mean them.
It sounds like a small distinction. In a room where four people are apologising, it is not.

readings.title: A Past Tense That Is Not About the Past
readings.setting: A page from a language guide
readings.passageScript:
English uses a past tense for two things that have nothing to do with the past.
The first is an unreal condition. If I had the time, I would rewrite it.
Nothing there is past. I am talking about today, and the past tense marks it as not true.
The second is a wish. I wish I knew what happened. Again the past tense, again about now.
This trips learners up because their instinct is to reach for a past meaning that is not there.
There is a useful way to see it. English shifts the tense back to signal distance.
Sometimes that distance is in time, which is the ordinary past.
Sometimes it is distance from reality, which is what these two are.
And sometimes it is social distance, which is why could you and would you are politer than can you and will you.
One tense, three kinds of distance.
The same shift explains something else. Were, rather than was, in if I were you.
That form survives only in this unreal use, which is why it sounds odd in any other sentence.
You will hear if I was you constantly. Were is what a careful writer uses, and it is worth the small effort.

readings.setting: The findings section of an internal review
readings.passageScript:
REVIEW FINDINGS — YARD INCIDENT, 14 NOVEMBER
Panel: three members. Findings agreed unanimously.

1. Cause
The trolley's brake had failed. It must have failed before the trolley was moved,
as it was found in the off position with no sign of use.
The second supplier can be ruled out; they made no delivery that week.

2. What ought to have happened
The temperature log should have been checked daily and was not.
The brake should have been tested at the monthly inspection.
The panel finds these to be failures of the procedure, not of any individual.

3. What could not reasonably have been foreseen
The brake had passed its last recorded test. Nobody could have foreseen its failure
from the information available at the time.

4. Mitigation
Three staff attended within a minute, which mitigated the damage considerably.
No injury resulted.

5. Accountability
The yard supervisor is accountable for the log. The panel does not find them negligent.
If the log had been checked, the failure would probably have been found earlier.

6. Recommendation
Brakes are to be tested weekly, in order not to rely on the monthly inspection alone.

grammar.title: If I had the time, I would do it: the unreal present
grammar.explanation:
Unit 5 taught you the two real conditionals, and said explicitly that the
third was not its job. This is the third.
It talks about NOW, or about any time, and it says the thing is not true.
The form looks past. The meaning is not.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
IF + past simple, THEN would + plain verb.

If I had the time, I would rewrite it.   (I do not have the time)
If it were cheaper, we would order more.  (it is not cheaper)
What would you do if they refused?       (they have not refused)

Compare it with the first conditional, which you have:
If it rains tomorrow, I will take the bus.   (it may well rain)
If it rained every day, I would move.        (it does not)
The past tense is what marks it as unreal. Nothing about it is past.

WERE for all persons, in careful English:
If I were you, I would ask.
If it were cheaper. You will hear was; were is what an examiner wants.

COULD and MIGHT can replace would:
If we had the figures, we could decide today.
If we asked, they might agree.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Say this as an unreal condition: I do not have the time, so I am not rewriting it.
1. Is it true now? No, and that is the point.
2. Unreal takes the past simple in the if half: if I had the time.
3. The other half takes would plus a plain verb: I would rewrite it.
Answer: If I had the time, I would rewrite it.
If I have the time, I will rewrite it would mean I might well have it.
grammar.commonMistake:
would never appears in the if half, in the same way will never did.
No: If I would have the time, I would rewrite it.
Yes: If I had the time, I would rewrite it.
One half carries would. It is not the half with if in it.
grammar.memoryTip: The past tense marks it as unreal, not as past. And no would after if.

grammar.title: I wish I knew: complaining without accusing anybody
grammar.explanation:
This is new, and it uses the same trick as the card before it.
A past tense, meaning now, marking something as not true.
wish is how English complains about the present without complaining about
anybody, which makes it extremely useful at work.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
WISH + past simple, about a fact you want changed:
I wish I knew what happened.     (I do not know)
I wish it were simpler.          (it is not)
I wish we had more time.         (we do not)

WISH + could, about an ability:
I wish I could help.             (I cannot)

WISH + WOULD, about somebody else's behaviour. This one is a complaint:
I wish they would reply.         (they are not replying, and it annoys me)
I wish he would stop doing that.
You cannot use would about yourself: not I wish I would know.

IF ONLY does the same job, more strongly:
If only we had the figures.

Note what wish does NOT mean here. I wish you a good journey is a different
verb altogether, and takes no clause of this kind.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Complain that nobody has replied, without accusing anybody.
1. Is this about a fact, or about somebody's behaviour? Their behaviour.
2. Behaviour you want changed takes wish + would.
3. I wish they would reply.
Answer: I wish they would reply.
I wish they replied would be about a general fact, which is not what you mean,
and why have they not replied accuses them directly.
grammar.commonMistake:
wish + would cannot be used about yourself, because you control your own behaviour.
No: I wish I would know.
Yes: I wish I knew.
Use the past simple for yourself, and would only for other people.
grammar.memoryTip: Past simple for a fact. would for somebody else's behaviour. Never would about yourself.

3. I wish we had more time.  4. I wish I could help.
5. I wish they would reply.  6. I wish he would stop interrupting.
7. I wish I knew what happened.  8. I wish it WERE simpler.

grammar.title: It must be the seal: working out what is true
grammar.explanation:
You have met must, might and can't as permission, obligation and ability.
They have a completely separate job, and no card below this one touches it.
They say how certain you are that something IS the case, from the evidence.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
MUST be     = I am nearly certain it is
  It must be the seal. Nothing else touches that line.
MIGHT / MAY / COULD be = it is possible
  It might be the seal, or it might be the gasket.
CAN'T be    = I am nearly certain it is not
  It can't be the supplier. They did not deliver that week.

Note what is NOT here: mustn't. The opposite of must be is CAN'T be.
mustn't be means it is forbidden, which is a different job entirely.

ABOUT THE PAST, add have plus the participle:
It must have been the seal.
It can't have been the supplier.
It might have been either.

These are all DEDUCTIONS, not facts. They tell the reader how you got there.
The seal failed          states a finding
It must have been the seal  states a deduction from evidence
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
The supplier did not deliver that week. How sure are you they are not involved?
1. Do you have evidence? Yes, and it rules them out.
2. Near certainty that something is NOT so takes can't be.
3. Not mustn't be, which would mean they are forbidden.
Answer: It can't be the supplier. They did not deliver that week.
About the past: it can't have been the supplier.
grammar.commonMistake:
mustn't is not the opposite of must, in this job.
No: It mustn't be the supplier. (that says they are forbidden to be it)
Yes: It can't be the supplier.
must be and can't be are the pair. mustn't belongs to the other job.
grammar.memoryTip: must be, might be, can't be. Add have for the past. mustn't is not in this set.
grammar.practice:

3. They did not deliver that week. (the supplier, near certain not)
4. The same thing happened last year, so it was probably the seal then too. (past)
5. Nobody was on site, so the supplier was definitely not there. (past)
Now correct these.
6. It mustn't be the supplier; they did not deliver.
7. It must been the seal.
grammar.answerKey:
1. It must be the seal.  2. It might be the seal or the gasket.
3. It can't be the supplier.  4. It must have been the seal.
5. It can't have been the supplier.
6. It can't be the supplier.  7. It must HAVE been the seal.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: I should have checked: regret, and criticism
grammar.explanation:
This is the form English uses to say something was not done that ought to
have been. It is new, and it does two jobs that feel very different: it
apologises, and it accuses. The grammar is identical for both.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
SHOULD HAVE + past participle = it did not happen, and it ought to have.
I should have checked the log.      (I did not)
We should have anticipated it.      (we did not)

SHOULDN'T HAVE = it did happen, and it ought not to have.
He shouldn't have moved the trolley. (he did)

OUGHT TO HAVE means the same and is more formal:
The log ought to have been checked daily.

COULD HAVE = it was possible and did not happen.
We could have ordered earlier.
It carries less blame than should have.

The passive removes the person, exactly as in Unit 10:
I should have checked the log.      names me
The log should have been checked.   names nobody
In a report, that choice is the whole difference between an apology and a
finding. Make it on purpose.

And with hindsight, everything looks like a should have. Be careful.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You did not check the log, and you ought to have. Write it two ways.
1. The action did not happen and ought to have: should have.
2. Naming yourself: I should have checked the log.
3. Naming nobody: the log should have been checked.
Answer: both are correct, and they are not the same sentence.
The first is an apology. The second is a finding about a procedure.
grammar.commonMistake:
should have is easy to write about other people from a position of hindsight.
Weak: They should have foreseen it. (could anybody have?)
Fairer: They could have ordered earlier. Or: nobody could have foreseen it.
Hindsight makes everything look obvious. The word for that is hindsight.
grammar.memoryTip: should have = it did not happen and ought to. The passive decides whether you are naming anybody.
grammar.practice:

1. I did not check the log, and I ought to have.
2. He moved the trolley, and he ought not to have.
3. We did not order earlier, though it was possible. (less blame)
4. Nobody anticipated the second failure, and they ought to have.
Now rewrite 1 and 4 in the passive, and say what changes.
5. Say that nobody could have known, as a defence.
grammar.answerKey:
1. I should have checked the log.  2. He shouldn't have moved the trolley.
3. We could have ordered earlier.  4. They should have anticipated it.
1 passive: The log should have been checked. 4 passive: The second failure
should have been anticipated. Both now name nobody, so they read as findings
about a procedure rather than as blame.
5. Nobody could have foreseen it.
5 or more right: good.

grammar.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
grammar.title: So as not to, in case: saying what for
grammar.explanation:
Unit 7 gave you so that, for purpose. Unit 6 gave you although and however,
for contrast. What neither covered is the rest of the purpose set, and in
particular how to say what you did something to AVOID.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
PURPOSE, positive:
in order to + plain verb   We rang in order to confirm the date.
so as to + plain verb      We rang so as to confirm it.
to + plain verb            We rang to confirm it.   (the everyday one)
so that + a clause         We rang so that everybody knew.

PURPOSE, negative. This is the part that is new:
in order NOT to + plain verb    We left early in order not to miss it.
so as NOT to + plain verb       We left early so as not to miss it.
NOT: we left early for not miss it, or to not miss it.

IN CASE is different, and learners use it for purpose by mistake:
We took a spare IN CASE the first one failed.
  = because it MIGHT fail, so we prepared beforehand
We took a spare SO THAT we could replace it.
  = that was the aim
in case is about a possibility. so that is about an aim.
And in case never takes will: in case it rains, not in case it will rain.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You left early because the train might have been full. Which one?
1. Was a full train your AIM, or a possibility you prepared for?
2. A possibility you prepared for.
3. That is in case, not so that.
Answer: We left early in case the train was full.
We left early so as not to miss the train is also correct, and it says
something slightly different: missing it was what you were avoiding.
grammar.commonMistake:
The negative purpose is where this goes wrong, in both directions.
No: We left early for not missing it.
No: We left early to not miss it.
Yes: We left early so as not to miss it. Or: in order not to miss it.
grammar.memoryTip: so as not to for what you are avoiding. in case for what might happen.
grammar.practice:
Choose in order to, so as not to, so that or in case.
1. We rang ___ confirm the date.
2. We left early ___ miss the train.
3. We took a spare ___ the first one failed.
4. We rang ___ everybody knew.
5. We wrote it down ___ forget it.
6. Take a coat ___ it rains.
Now correct these.
7. We left early for not missing it.
8. Take a coat in case it will rain.
grammar.answerKey:
1. in order to  2. so as not to  3. in case  4. so that
5. so as not to  6. in case
7. We left early so as not to miss it.
8. Take a coat in case it rains. (in case never takes will)
3 and 6 are possibilities prepared for; 1, 2, 4 and 5 are aims.
6 or more right: good.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — The would that shrinks to a d
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
In a second conditional, would is almost never stressed. It shrinks to a d
and joins on to the word in front.

we would ORder more       sounds like  we-d ORder more

activities.title: Practice 6 — How certain does it sound?
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Each sentence states something as a flat fact. Rewrite it at the strength the
evidence actually supports, using a word from group 1 or a modal.
1. The brake was faulty. (you were told, and have not checked)
2. Nobody checked the log. (it is unsigned for three weeks)
3. The supplier delivered the wrong batch. (they deny it, nothing is proved)
4. The line was checked on Monday. (somebody says so and you doubt it)
5. Both failed at the same time. (possible, but unlikely)
activities.answerSummary:
Yours will differ. Each should match the evidence you were given.
1. Apparently the brake was faulty. (you heard it; you did not see it)
2. Presumably nobody checked the log. Or: nobody can have checked it.
3. The supplier allegedly delivered the wrong batch.
4. The line was supposedly checked on Monday. (supposedly carries your doubt)
5. It is conceivable that both failed at once.
Note the pair in 3 and 4: allegedly is neutral, supposedly is not.
4 or 5 right: good.

activities.title: Practice 7 — Find it in the findings
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Answer from Reading 3 only.
1. What evidence supports the deduction about when the brake failed?
2. Who is ruled out, and why?
3. Is the yard supervisor found negligent?
4. Copy two should-have sentences and say whether they name anybody.
5. Copy the second conditional and say what it claims.
6. Copy the phrase in section 6 that gives a negative purpose.
activities.answerSummary:
1. It was found in the off position with no sign of use.
2. The second supplier: they made no delivery that week.
3. No. They are accountable for the log, but not found negligent.
4. 'The temperature log should have been checked daily' and 'The brake should
   have been tested at the monthly inspection.' Both passive; neither names anybody.
5. 'If the log had been checked, the failure would probably have been found earlier.'
   It claims that checking was not done, and that doing it would have changed the outcome.
6. 'in order not to rely on the monthly inspection alone'.
5 or 6 right: good.

assignments.title: The findings, and what hindsight added
assignments.instructions:
Part one. Write the findings of a review into something that went wrong, in six
sections and about 170 words: Cause, What ought to have happened, What could not
have been foreseen, Mitigation, Accountability, Recommendation.
Cause must use two modals of deduction with their evidence, and rule one thing out.
Section 2 must be passive throughout. Section 5 must separate accountable for from
negligent. The recommendation must use a negative purpose.
Part two. Rewrite section 2 naming individuals instead, and write two sentences on
what changes for the person reading it.
Part three. Write four sentences beginning 'If ... had ...' about what would have
happened differently, and one sentence beginning 'Nobody could have foreseen'.
Then write one sentence saying which of your should-have findings is unfair with
hindsight, and why.
